questions.question: Give an account on dehiscent and indehiscent fruits. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Give an account on dehiscent and indehiscent fruits. [U] / [CO1]
  • Ans. Dehiscent - Legume: splits along two sutures (e.g., pea)
  • Follicle: splits along one suture (e.g., Calotropis)
  • Capsule: splits in various ways (e.g., cotton)
  • Siliqua/Silicula: characteristic of mustard family
  • Indehiscent - Achene: single-seeded, free pericarp (e.g., sunflower)
  • Caryopsis: seed coat fused with pericarp (e.g., wheat)
  • Nut: hard, woody pericarp (e.g., cashew)
  • Drupe: fleshy outer part with hard stone (e.g., mango, coconut)

questions.question: What is sorosis? Explain with suitable example? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is sorosis? Explain with suitable example? [U] / [CO1]
  • Ans. Sorosis is a type of multiple fruit that develops from a spike or spadix inflorescence,
  • where the entire inflorescence (flowers, axis, and sometimes bracts) fuses together to form a
  • single, large fruit.
  • Ananas comosus (Pineapple) –the axis and flowers fuse into a juicy mass.
  • Artocarpus heterophyllus (Jackfruit) – develops from a spike.
  • Rachis (axis): Thick, fibrous central core.
  • Edible portion: Consists of fleshy yellow bulbs. Each bulb develops from the perianth of
  • individual flowers.
  • Seeds: Each bulb encloses a single large seed.
  • Fibrous strands: Non-edible, thread-like structures derived from unfertilized flowers.
  • Morus (Mulberry) – formed from a catkin inflorescence.

questions.question: What is a fruit? Give an account on simple fruits. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is a fruit? Give an account on simple fruits. [K] / [CO1]
  • Ans. A fruit is a matured ovary of a flower formed after fertilization, containing seeds. Sometimes, other floral
  • parts may also contribute to fruit formation (accessory fruits).
  • Simple fruits develop from the single ovary of a single flower. They may be dry or fleshy, depending on the
  • nature of the pericarp.
  • Dry Simple Fruits
  • Dehiscent fruits (split open at maturity)
  • Legume: Splits along two sutures (e.g., pea)
  • Follicle: Splits along one suture (e.g., Calotropis)
  • Capsule: Opens in different ways (e.g., cotton)
  • Siliqua: Long fruit of mustard family
  • Indehiscent fruits (do not split)
  • Split into mericarp units
  • Examples: coriander, castor
  • Fleshy Simple Fruits
  • Drupe -Outer fleshy part with hard inner stone
  • Example: mango, coconut
  • Berry - Entire pericarp fleshy
  • • Example: tomato, grape, banana
  • Pome- Fleshy thalamus forms edible part
  • • Example: apple, pea.
  • Pepo – Cucurbita.

questions.question: With the help of a labelled diagram explain the inflorescence of Poaceae. / [CO3] [10x1 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• With the help of a labelled diagram explain the inflorescence of Poaceae. [U] / [CO3]
  • Ans. The inflorescence in Poaceae is composed of spikelets, which are the basic units.
  • Each spikelet consists of:
  • Glumes
  • o Two sterile bracts at the base of the spikelet.
  • o Protect the developing florets.
  • Rachilla
  • o The central axis of the spikelet on which florets are arranged.
  • Florets
  • o Each floret is a small flower enclosed by:
  • • Lemma (outer bract, often with an awn)
  • • Palea (inner bract)
  • Lodicules
  • o Small scale-like structures (represent reduced perianth).
  • o Help in opening of the floret during flowering.
  • Androecium
  • o Usually 3 stamens with versatile anthers.
  • Gynoecium
  • o Superior ovary, unilocular with a single ovule.
  • o Feathery stigmas for wind pollination.
  • [10x1 = 10]
